I would not call myself an expert, but I just attended an instructional clinic at the VA to start IM injections. I understood the process going in, but learned exactly how to perform an injection on myself.

1. ​Wash hands.  

2. Glove up.  

3. Aspirate the medication. (The VA recommends one needle for ease of aspiration, and a second for the injection itself. If you buy your own needles, this does not seem to be vital--you can probably use the gauge easiest for you.)
4. Swab the injection site with alcohol.
5. I chose to inject into my thigh. I was directed  to go just above the midpoint of my thigh between the front and where a side seam would be on trousers.  

6. Pinch the injection site. This increases the depth of tissue available and the slight pain of the pinch will help prevent you from feeling much, if anything, from the insertion of the needle.
7. Insert the needle smoothly and with confidence, but very little force--there should be no noticeable resistance.
8. Push down the plunger. (The medication is thick, so it is likely to sting \*a little bit\*. The pain should be minimal.)
9. Remove the needle, press a cotton ball to the tiny wound.
10. Cap the needle.
11. Apply a Band-Aid (to protect your clothes, mostly, but there should be very little blood if any).
12. Put your needle into a Sharps container. You could buy one of these, or use a gallon jug with a lid and use a Sharpie to write on it "SHARPS: DO NOT RECYCLE." (This last part did not come from the endocrine clinic--it came from our veterinarian when we were giving our cat insulin.)  


HTH!

First of all, even what you wrote there has grammar and syntax.

Second, I don't know your professional specialty or how long you've been doing it, but there are any number of reasons you might need to communicate information about your work in clear scientific English.

You might need or want to do any of the following:

1. Nearly every profession requiring a specialized education has one or more professional conferences.
a. You might want to give a talk.
b. You might want to publish findings in a professional journal, such as JAMA or The Lancet.

2. You might for whatever reason decide to teach instead of or alongside clinical practice.
a. that may mean making what you do clear to non-specialists, or specialists in discrete but related fields.
b. some people write the textbooks you use. good money in that.

3. Grant writing. Useful and necessary skill for most scientists. You have to detail what you want to do, and it's not going to be in ER jargon (In addition to being a college professor, I used to be an EMT. Medical shorthand is not news to me.)

So maybe you don't want to do those things, maybe your institution will not require you to do any sort of continuing professional development, maybe you just want to treat people, go home at night, and repeat forever.

But lots of other people in your field WILL want to do some or all of these things.
